cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Hand It Over
cards.instruction: Persuade someone to give up control of a task, object, or decision you believe is being mishandled.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. Let me fix that cupboard hinge. The door's lower than when you started.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: I'm just finding the right screw.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. You've tried four. Give me the screwdriver while you find it.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Then you'll tell everyone you fixed it.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can announce the repair. I'll stand behind you with the screwdriver, keeping the door attached.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 takes decision authority over a worsening hinge, A3 demands the tool, and A5 grants B announcement rights while reserving actual repair control.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 screw search causes A3 count of failed tries; B4 credit fear causes A5 split between announcing and holding the screwdriver.

relationship.evidence: B2 explains the method and B4 protects credit, giving A a practical and personal objection to address.

heightening.evidence: B4 status concern becomes A5 a concession that lets B keep public credit while A controls the fix.

specificity.evidence: A1 lowered cupboard door and A3 four attempted screws make A belief in mishandling specific.
